title: Work-related aggravation — ignore or address? WWYD? | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "nutsaboutplants", "author_name": "nutsaboutplants", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/nutsaboutplants", "date": "2025-12-01", "text": "A young colleague\u2019s LinkedIn post a couple of weeks ago has been niggling at me for various reasons. This colleague, let\u2019s call them Alex, posts with great enthusiasm about their work and lists the various things they do. Included in this list is drafting of bills. (Alex is the legislative liaison for our employer.) While Alex would reasonably be expected to draft bills in their role, they do not in reality draft bills. Ever. I do. Some background info relevant to the situation: I used to be the general counsel for my employer as well as the legislative liaison until I retired about 5 years ago. During my absence, my employer hired a general counsel. The employee also hired, separately, a legislative liaison. Neither person worked out. About 3 years ago, the employer wooed me out of retirement. And I was really feeling the lack of intellectual stimulation and agreed to come back on one condition: I didn\u2019t want to do legislative work. The employer said, no worries, we have this young person who\u2019s itching to do that work. That was Alex. I said great and went back. I do enjoy being back because I love the law, the stimulation, most of my coworkers, etc. It turns out Alex defines their role fairly narrowly and doesn\u2019t do bill drafting, review all bills filed to asess the potential impact on the employer/industry, or monitor amendments. Alex goes to the capitol, works at developing and maintaining relationships with legislators, and communicates with relevant folks. I am so relieved that I don\u2019t have to do this glad-handling part and that Alex is good at this. This, to me, was the least enjoyable aspect of the legislative work and am glad to have someone who enjoys doing it. But it\u2019s been a little irritating to me that Alex will not engage with bill drafting. I don\u2019t mind that work, and can do it well, but don\u2019t enjoy it. Another relevant fact \u2014 Alex doesn\u2019t report to me. I report directly to the head. Alex reports to someone else a couple of levels down. In my 30 year career, I\u2019ve hired, trained, mentored about 100 or so young attorneys like Alex. But in my current role with this employer, Alex doesn\u2019t report to me. And at this stage in my career, this job is just a lagniappe to me both in terms of our finances and my reputation. I truly don\u2019t care if people think Alex is drafting our bills rather than me. I came out of retirement mainly because I like my work and was bored out of my mind. So, this LinkedIn post where Alex lists with great enthusiasm the various things they do and enjoy about their work, including bill-drafting, came on top of my three years of mild irritation about why Alex\u2019s job has been allowed to be construed narrowly to exclude bill-drafting. I had two competing reactions to this post: to treat Alex as I would any other young attorney under my tutelage and counsel them that it\u2019s not a good thing to inflate their work,  that any reputation must be earned and should stand on solid work that one does do. (If I did counsel them, I would have noted the excellent job they are doing in all other aspects of their role and that bill-drafting would round that out nicely. In other words, the advice would be constructive, not meant to diminish what they do.) The second reaction was just to ignore the whole thing. Why bother? (Actually, even the 10 minutes it has taken to write this seems a waste of time and effort.) WWYD?", "images": []}
other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "pricklypearcactus", "author_name": "pricklypearcactus", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/pricklypearcactus", "date": "2025-12-01", "text": "I would not recommend approaching Alex about anything related to his LinkedIn post. I would focus on making certain that you and your boss are aligned on your responsibilities. If drafting bills is beyond the scope of work that you agreed to return to, that could be worth a conversation with your boss. Though I would approach with caution, as the boss may need someone in your role willing to draft bills, so you could jeopardize your position by pushing back. I would not discuss Alex directly in the conversation as his responsibilities are really irrelevant to the conversation. On a personal level, I would absolutely be bothered by someone else publicly claiming responsibility for the work I'd done. Unforunately, I believe it is somewhat common for young professionals to be encouraged to stretch the truth (or blatantly lie) on resumes and LinkedIn to improve their chances for advancement. It sits at about 32\" over the cooktop, which is higher than recommended. It doesn't do a great job at capturing exhaust, especially from the front burners. The next obvious thing to do would be to start over completely from scratch and remodel the entire framed construction above it so that it sits lower. We would go just wide enough to cover the insert, so presumably we would end up with some wood trim around it but smaller than the current perimeter. This would work, but might look weird. Idea 2: Get an under-cabinet hood. We would just push the under-cabinet hood partway into the opening vacated by the current insert. We'd build some minimal additional support up inside that opening to attach the top of the hood to. This is much simpler and cheaper than Idea 1. Island hoods seem to be expensive, so maybe this wouldn't pay, and might be too big and prominent for that spot. I'm also not sure if this kind of installation could be done. title: Milwaukee, WI Winter Rose protection....YIKES | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "nickjoseph", "author_name": "nickjoseph Milwaukee, WI", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/nickjoseph", "date": "2025-12-05", "text": "I typically put a collar around my 10 roses bushes against the south side of our brick home & fill them 1/2-to maybe a little more with mulch.  I do this by December 10th.  Well, the weather did not cooperate with us.  Couldn't do it before December 1st cuz the November weather was in the 40s & 50s.  Saturday 11-29, got hit with wet, sloppy 8\" of snow.  Couldn't do the collars with that.  Now today temps hit 14\u00b0.  Am I screwed cuz haven't covered yet?  Thanks.", "images": []}
other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "paul-barden62", "author_name": "Paul Barden", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/paul-barden62", "date": "2025-12-14", "text": "When I was a teenager living in a much colder climate than the one I live in now, many gardeners bought into the whole \"winterize your roses\" concept (a concept I believe was manufactured by the companies that made the winterization technologies that were being promoted), myself included. Yeah, I'd buy those paper or plastic cones and collars and heap up soil 8\" deep around the crown, cover with leaves, etc, etc. Many roses barely survived the winter anyway. (I remember both 'Tiffany' and 'Peace' survived 2 or 3 winters at most) But at some point I stopped doing it because it was tedious and I became involved in other things. Ya know what? It turns out it did not make one bit of difference if I did or didn't \"winterize\" the roses I had. The ones that were least suited to the climate died after 1, 2 or 3 years, and the ones that were appropriate for that climate did just fine without any fuss. I still have a piece of the original 'Hansa' my grandmother and I planted when I was about 14. Yah, don't ask how long ago that was! I would say that if someone has established roses that are ten to thirty years old that prosper in the climate they're grown in, then they are sufficiently hardy for that zone and winterizing those roses is probably completely unnecessary \u2014 it's more of a case of the gardener feeling that they are actively participating in the survival of those roses. But I seriously doubt that any rose that has lived thirty years where they are planted, requires any special handling to get them through the winter. But do whatever makes you feel that you're doing the right thing for your garden. No one else has the authority to dictate our garden techniques or our choices. Do what makes you happy.", "images": []}}

title: Frigidaire Gallery GRQ2255BF 4 door Freezer Temp fluctuations | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "thundley", "author_name": "thundley", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/thundley", "date": "2025-12-06", "text": "My battle with new fridge and freezer temp fluctuations continues.  This is the quad door model with two freezer sections on the bottom (One is convertible, but that is not really relevant here). I have been monitoring the temp in the freezer with the Govee system, which sends data back to my phone app.  Even though I have the freezer set to -2, the temp in the freezer still fluctuates between -3F and 9F, with 2-3 dramatic spikes throughout the day.  Even when doors are kept closed. On the other side of the ditch, a plant of 'Reve d'Or', just above it an oak a few years old, above that rose 'Dumortier' and then a lilac, with Oregon grape growing between rose and lilac, and in front of 'Reve d'Or'. title: Only starting to figure it out: Protein | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "anniedeighnaugh", "author_name": "Annie Deighnaugh", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/anniedeighnaugh", "date": "2025-12-07", "text": "So with returning to WW and using their new phone app, I discovered that if I track all my foods, it totes up the total by macronutrients for me: protein, carb, fat, sat fat, etc. but it's in grams. From the old WW days, my rule of thumb was 1 ounce of protein at breakfast, 2 at lunch and 3 at dinner for 6 ounces per day, so like 1 egg at breakfast, 2 oz of turkey at lunch and 3 oz of poultry/meat/fish at dinner.  But when I looked at the totals and their target, I was only about halfway there.  They target roughly 75-110 grams of protein per day.  When I toted up what they said I ate, they were right, and it's well below the quantity of protein I thought I was eating. 1 ounce of chicken is 28 g, so 3 ounces would be plenty right?  Except that chicken is more than just protein.  And there's the rub.  Egg is more than just protein.  So 53g egg is not 53g of protein.  Rather an egg is 5g fat, 1g carb and 6g protein (I'm assuming the rest is shell?)  So why am I only figuring this out now??? I've been losing weight steadily and feeling fairly satiated most of the time now, so I don't want to mess with success.  But I am going to have to look into upping my protein... main_question: {"author_id": "carl-celle", "author_name": "Carl Celle", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/carl-celle", "date": "2025-12-08", "text": "UPDATE: Thank you all sincerely for the invaluable feedback and diverse perspectives shared on this thread. The discussion has been highly informative, and I believe future readers will find a wealth of useful advice here. Ultimately, due to the complex variables and timeline requirements involved, we've determined that our current home is not the optimal fit for this specific type of addition. We genuinely appreciate the time you took to contribute your insights. Thank you again. ///////////////////////////////////////////// Hello everyone, My wife and I are embarking on a major project and desperately need the collective wisdom of this community! My wife's parents, both in their 80s, can no longer live on their own, and we are planning to have them move in with us. We want to create a comfortable, accessible, and semi-independent space for them. QUESTION: Can you give us any advice on layout, square footage needed or things to be mindful of? We are thinking the east side of the house BUT are open to other ideas. LINK TO FLOORPLAN: https://drive.google.com/file/d/1OUOJlOVcjageIOzQhQYwD1H84UtsHhog/view?usp=sharing The Goal: One bedroom. The Challenge: Constraints and Location Our Current Thinking (The Narrow Addition): Given the 11-foot maximum width, we anticipate having to build a very long, narrow addition, likely running the length of a significant portion of the house (a \"shotgun\" or linear style). Thank you in advance for any insights, sketches, or previous project examples you can share. This is a huge step for our family!", "images": []}
other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "kendrahhendra", "author_name": "Kendrah", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/kendrahhendra", "date": "2025-12-08", "text": "Wonderful that you are open to multi-generational living. I cannot read your plan.  Can you post it as another kind of file?  And, can you outline in a color the area where you wish to build? Two years ago, we created a suite, including kitchenette for my parents in their 80s should they ever need to come live with us.  I did loads of research including hiring an occupational therapist design specialist, and consulted my Dad, who has worked as an engineer on over 100 buildings that are ADA compliant. Falls are the most significant factor in precipitating decline in the elderly.  You want minimize fall risk in every decision you make.  Having wide, easy walking pathways is very important.  And you will need additional width to all circulation pathways to accommodate walker usage should they need one. You want to reduce distance needed to walk to the bathroom.  Urgency and frequency become issues with age and you don't want to create a long walk to the bathroom that encourages hurrying and increases fall risk. Consider how well you can achieve these needs in an 11 foot width shotgun layout.  The words LONG and NARROW are immediate red flags.  Perhaps you can think more creatively about where they should dwell.  Maybe they live in the primary suite and you and your spouse live in this new addition?  Or some other such swapping of space. Think hard about this. Also... 1. Do not build a bathroom to ADA specs.  They are created to suit the common denominator -- the average person in the general public.  Instead, base your height and spacing on the actual needs and height of your in-laws. Do they have degenerative diseases that will likely result in wheelchair usage?  If not, then don't build for wheelchair.  Only 7% of seniors end up needing a wheel chair.  Instead install grab bars for THEIR arm reach height, place sinks at THEIR height needs.  Allow enough room in a bathroom for a caregiver to assist with toileting and shower, room to park walkers, etc. 2. Have doors open out instead of into a room.  Should they fall and block a doorway, you don't want them trapped inside. 3. Get apple watches for them that will alert you if they have fallen.  You can live in the same house and still not hear someone yelling in the night because they have fallen. 4. Excellent daytime and nighttime lighting is key to reducing falls. There are loads of other tips to making a senior friendly living space but they are cart before the horse at this stage of your planning.", "images": []}}

We're concerned having four seams on the deck will ruin the look, not to mention we've seen really bad seams on here and are afraid we may become another victim of those. Would like to hear from other fabricators, designers, and home owners. Not sure if it's just something beyond this fabricator's capability, they're wanting to take the easy way, or if it's something with which most fabricators would agree. For added insurance, the GC went ahead and beefed up the front side of the deck a bit more and the fabricator thought that would help as well. The reason I'm using past tense is -- it's done! title: Diablo IV Season 11: Divine Gifts And Sanctification Explained | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "fc26-coins", "author_name": "fc26 coins", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/fc26-coins", "date": "2025-12-11", "text": "In this article, we'll introduce the key update for the new season, Divine Gifts, and reveal the release date of Diablo IV Season 11 Divine Intervention.Release Date And Divine Gifts IntroductionSeason 11 Divine Intervention is scheduled to launch on Tuesday, December 12th, 2025, at 10:00 AM. The brand-new season mechanic, Divine gifts, will also be launched simultaneously.  In short, Diablo IV Season 11 allows players to modify and enhance their abilities through season-specific temporary powers\u2014this is Divine Gifts!As a new season mechanic, Divine Gifts operates similarly to previous versions, using a slot system similar to previous seasons. However, it doesn't aim to directly increase character strength, but rather enhances rewards for specific events. While different players may have different opinions, Divine Gifts will increase the rewards from open-world content, and players can control and obtain more of the rewards they need through their choices. Compared to simply and directly boosting character strength, this is undoubtedly a bold attempt, bringing players a fresh gaming experience.Corrupted And PurifiedDivine Gifts will come in two forms: Corrupted and Purified. Corrupted Gifts will increase the difficulty of monsters, giving them more mechanics and significantly increasing the game's challenge, but will still provide a Divine Gift reward bonus. If you felt the previous versions weren't difficult enough, this gift might offer a minor challenge. The second type, Purified Gifts, will remove the negative effects of Corrupted Gifts and provide additional game buffs, doubling the related rewards. This is undoubtedly a very attractive buff, allowing players to more easily and quickly obtain game rewards to enhance their character's strength.Please note that each Divine Gift contains three parts: the corresponding reward, the Corrupted Gift form, and the Purified Gift form. After defeating a lower-level evil and obtaining the corresponding Divine Gifts for its Corrupted Essence, the Corrupted Gift slot will be automatically unlocked; the Purification Gift slot requires increasing your Divine Gifts Season reputation level.New Item Mechanics: Tempering, Masterworking & SanctificationTempering: Finally, you can pick the exact affixes you want\u2014and revert changes anytime. No more wasting materials on unwanted rolls. It\u2019s a game-changer for building personalized, min-maxed gear.Masterworking: This allows you to directly enhance an item\u2019s quality. Once you hit max quality, you unlock a Capstone Bonus, upgrading regular affixes to powerful Greater Affixes. It\u2019s a clear, satisfying path to strengthening your gear\u2014no guesswork, just steady progress.Sanctification is the final stage of Masterworking and the last step in that stage. As the pinnacle of the item crafting process, Sanctification imbues the item with a small amount of Celestial Power, randomly drawn from a range of possible upgrade options. After sanctification, the item cannot be modified in any way, so any tempering or reforging must be completed before this step. Sanctification is the final step in perfecting your gear, meaning you'll need to prepare a significant amount of resources or buy Diablo 4 items beforehand. Completed sanctification will have five possible effects:1. Add a new Legendary Aspect (creating dual-Aspect gear)2. Convert one affix to an Ancestral-tier roll3. Add a brand-new sanctified affix4. Randomly turn one existing affix into a sanctified one5. Make the gear so that it never loses durabilityThe new mechanics bring new challenges and experiences, so please look forward to the arrival of the new season, Divine Intervention!", "images": []}

other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "3katz4me", "author_name": "3katz4me", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/3katz4me", "date": "2025-12-11", "text": "From Google AI: Here are the primary reasons why your freezer temperature might only rise noticeably at night: 1. \u2744\ufe0f The Automatic Defrost Cycle All modern frost-free freezers and refrigerators must periodically warm up to melt any frost buildup on the evaporator coils.1 This is the defrost cycle. Timed Cycles: The defrost cycle is typically controlled by a timer or a circuit board and is often programmed to run at regular, fixed intervals, such as every 8, 10, 12, or 24 hours.2 Night-Time Scheduling: Manufacturers often schedule the defrost cycle to run when the refrigerator is least likely to be opened, which is usually overnight. This minimizes the impact of the temporary temperature increase on your food, as the doors aren't being opened to let in more warm air while the freezer is already warming up. Observed Rise: During the defrost cycle, a heating element warms the coils to melt the ice, causing the internal air temperature\u2014especially near the coils\u2014to rise for a short period (typically 20-45 minutes). If your freezer is not very full (lacking thermal mass from food), the air temperature will spike more dramatically.3 2. \ud83c\udf21\ufe0f External Factors Amplified Overnight While the defrost cycle is the most likely cause, other factors could contribute to a nighttime-only rise: 3. \u2699\ufe0f Possible Component Issues (If the Rise is Excessive) If the temperature rise is significant (e.g., above $10^\\circ \\text{F}$ and food is thawing), it could indicate a problem that is being exacerbated by the defrost cycle: \u2705 What to Check", "images": []}}

Well, the annual bloom cycle in my garden is at close to its minimum, and yet, I'm happy at what I see.  Part of it is that my garden helper is back after a wet week when he couldn't work, and he has been mowing.  It's amazing how mowing will beautify a garden, bringing it into focus.  Here much of the grass grows in the winter, and the smooth mown swathes of bright green are lovely, and lively, in themselves. I grew up in north Florida, a place with a four season climate and an abundance of evergreen and deciduous plants both wild and cultivated.  When I moved to the farm, the first thing I did after my first winter there was to plant box, because my eyes had been so starved for green during the winter.  There is very little native evergreen growth here. The box was followed over time by sarcococca, photinia, bay laurel (a mistake, that), Leyland cypress, cotoneaster, holm oak, olives, palms, and finally by Italian cypresses.  These are all pretty ornamental year 'round, but stand out particularly after leaf fall.  We use the Italian cypresses to outline the main walk down through the big garden, and to define focal points.  Some of these plants, like the brilliant Cotoneaster lacteus, fruit marvelously, with abundant bright red berries that last through the winter.  They offer contrasts of texture and color, for example the shifting smooth silver of the olives against the rough dark green of the cypresses.  There are also the subshrubs, plants like phlomis, shrub germander, rosemary, all evergreen, with their range of textures and greens. I like deciduous trees and shrubs that reveal good structure when their branches are bare, like oaks, flowering ash, Japanese persimmons.  The hedges are all mixed, as pure evergreen hedges are heavy, and, if they're monocultures, especially clones, boring.  Also a wasted opportunity, in my opinion.  Photinia as a monoculture is really dull, like plastic, but those glossy green leaves and new red growth are pretty wonderful mixed in with deciduous shrubs.  Also I like to see my hedge plants free in their growth rather than pruned into geometrical shapes. This is a busy work period in the garden, with planting going on until the end of the year (not beyond that, I hope) and much cleanup going on.  I've been pruning here and then, gently limbing up growing oaks, clearing grass around the bases of roses.  We've had some good weather this month (really too much:  ground water levels are low), pleasant for working outside, and blue skies and sun really dress up the place.  Of course, a good deal of the garden I see is in my mind, visualizing how it will be once the newly planted hazelnuts, roses, flowering ash, phlomis and sage and so forth have started growing well.  But even objectively, parts of the garden are looking good.  And there's plenty to do there, so it's never boring.  Next month the winter aconite and sarcococca and snowdrop will get going blooming, and by the end of February we'll have hellebores and sweet violets and snow crocuses, and it will just keep accelerating from there.  But even in December, the garden is just fine.", "images": []}

I decided not to use self-clean after reading about problems with electronics.  Have never used steam clean.  Tried to hand clean once with a baking soda solution. Rein \u00e4sthetisch finde ich, die Haube sollte als sichtbares Ger\u00e4t die Farben der Ger\u00e4te spiegeln, also Edelstahl/schwarz, oder so intergriert sein, dass sie sich optisch zu den Oberschr\u00e4nken oder Wand gesellt. Mein Problem ist, dass ich ein schwarzes Ger\u00e4t f\u00fcr unsere K\u00fcche zu wuchtig finde, und f\u00fcr eine integriete Version bisher keine gute L\u00f6sung gefunden habe. other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "pfvwus-pf~689457039", "author_name": "Raumagentur ArteFakt", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/professionals/pfvwus-pf~689457039", "date": "2026-01-05", "text": "Hallo und ein gutes neues Jahr :-) Erfahrungen habe ich mit Faber noch nicht gemacht, aber das Zusammenspiel von Hitzequelle, Thermik im Raum, Abstand zur Haube ist esentieller als deren Parameter. Bestm\u00f6glich sollte bei geringster Stufe schon eine Absaugwirkung gegeben sein. Induktion erhitzt eher die Speisen, so da\u00df wir weniger aufsteigende arme Luft haben als bei konventionellem Kochfeld, so da\u00df die Leistung der Haube schonmal h\u00f6her sein muss, um die gleiche Wirkung zu erzielen. Solange die Haube aber keine Deckenhaube ist sondern wie hier recht nah \u00fcber der Kochzone h\u00e4ngt, ist das bei den meisten auch gegeben. ***** DOWNDRAFT Ein Downdraft nimmt immer auch Fl\u00e4che auf dem Kochfeld ein, so da\u00df wir oft eine Feldbreite von 80 cm und mehr haben. Insbesondere bei Ihnen w\u00e4re das sehr ungl\u00fccklich, da zur Sp\u00fcle bereits wenig Platz gegeben ist. Alternativ w\u00e4re ein Abzug hinter dem Kochfeld m\u00f6glich. Beide aber ben\u00f6tigen Platz im Unterschrank darunter f\u00fcr die gef\u00fchrte Abluft unter den Sockelbereich, nach vorn zur Sockelblende hinaus. Dazu m\u00fcssten hier dann weniger tiefe Schubladen eingesetzt werden. Wohlm\u00f6glich entfiele auch die  obere Schublade, da die Ablufttechnik (Motor)  unterhalb des Kochfeldes ihren Platz einfordert. Ja, die Abluft k\u00f6nnte auch oben direkt in den Schrank (gegen die Wand) geblasen werden, aber da es prim\u00e4r Wasserdampf ist, der abgef\u00fchrt wird, hat der Berater auf jeden Fall recht, da\u00df das mittelfristig dei Wand sch\u00e4digen wird. ***** GESTALTUNG Wie ich in meinem ersten Beitrag schon angedeutet habe, gibt es zwei Ans\u00e4tze zur Gestaltung: wir verschmelzen die Haube mit der Architektur, oder wir betonen sie als Designmerkmal (Solit\u00e4r). Zwischen den Fenstern (den \"Augen des Geb\u00e4udes\") ist aber mMn der Platz so gering, da\u00df jede Haube mit mind. 60 cm Breite sich wie ein st\u00f6render Fremdk\u00f6rper einfach dazwischenschiebt. (Ihr letztes Foto zeigt ganz sch\u00f6n diesen schwarzen Fokus). Entsprechend w\u00fcrde ich bei einem Korpus bleiben, der nicht aus Holzwerkstoff wie ein M\u00f6bel erscheint, sondern der wie die Architektur aus Putz und Farbe geformt ist. Also keine Mobilie (Bewegliche), sondern Teil der Immobilie (Unbeweglichen). Nach oben bis in die Schr\u00e4ge reichend (zB. auf H\u00f6he der Oberschr\u00e4nke), und von unten (55 cm tief) nach oben auf vllt. 30 cm Tiefe verj\u00fcnged zulaufend. Ebenso von der unteren Breite (70?) auf eher 50 oder weniger nach oben in der Breite zulaufend. Wie eine Kamin-Esse - oder eben eine Nase zwischen den Augen des Hauses. Die vertikalen senkrechechten au\u00dfenkanten dann noch auf 2,5 cm Radius abgerundet. Das braucht keine gesonderte Unterkonstrultion, es wird lediglich die Gipskartonplatte weggeraspelt. Das Resultat ist ein weiches Licht und keine harte, wieder pr\u00e4sent im Raum stehende Schattenkante. title: Crazy root barrier idea - the reverse root barrier | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "upperbaygardener", "author_name": "UpperBayGardener (zone 7)", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/upperbaygardener", "date": "2025-12-18", "text": "We are all aware of using root barrier for things like running bamboos to keep them from spreading outwards. Has anybody done the reverse?  Put in a barrier to keep something from spreading in? Now that I've had a couple gingers survive last winter, which I'm calling a \"mini polar vortex\", I've gone ginger crazy and ordered a couple from Almost Eden.  The problem is finding spots with the required light shade. I've shifted a large clump of Toona 'Flamingo' away from a mixed bed, because it took over everything else planted there.  It is now being re-established in an area that will be 25 ft from any other plantings...the bare minimum, probably.  Any suckers in the 25 ft. border of lawn, of course, will just be persistently cut down by the mower.  I think I will just zap any suckers, over 25 ft away, with a selective or roundup, and I can safely assume that it won't transfer back to damage the main clump.  Obviously if I have to do this, I'll be very cautious at first. But now that I gotta find spots for the gingers, the clump of Toona is looking mighty damn useful for shade.  Because of their gangly habit, they seem to cast a consistent medium shade.  But then I would go back to the problem of it overwhelming a 'mixed bed', the whole reason I moved it. (Well, really killed off the old clump with glyphosate - covering the poor stuff that was being overwhelmed with black plastic trash bags - and transferred some divisions 60 ft away.  It worked - everything the Toona was engulfing survived!) What I'm thinking of doing is buying some 2 ft. deep plastic bamboo barrier, and putting it on the northeast corner of the intended Toona clump.  It will be easy to dig w/my backhoe.  It would be maybe 4-5' ft in diameter.  Then plant the ginger(s) inside this, protecting them from being overwhelmed by the Toona! It will also have the added benefit of partly keeping my mongrel, patchy lawn, that does contain some Poa trivialis, from invading the gingers, too. Open to thoughts on why this might not work.  As shadows lengthen during the hottest part of the day, the Toonas will shade them. (Gingers due north might cause them to be too shaded - I discovered this can be a problem with my 'Pink V' that are under Taxodium 'Banita'.  I had to cut down some big branches to give it more sun.  OTOH, they clearly can't quite deal with full sun, even \"up\" here.  And, FWIW, I believe evergreen shade is mostly out of the question, cuz the rhizomes needs the warmth of sun in winter, given they are of borderline root hardiness.)", "images": []}

I am sure that the inmates appreciated the food you prepared. I understand your feelings toward people who are incarcerated.   At one time I may have expressed very similar feelings, but life experience has taught me to have a different perspective.    The largest incarcerated population when segmented into social risk factors is illiterate.   70 to 80 percent of the incarcerated population in the US can't read at a 4th grade level.   Between 10 and 46 percent can be diagnosed as having Fetal Alcohol Syndrome, and they estimate approximately 60% of inmates are living with Traumatic Brain Injury, many from childhood abuse, so they have impaired impulse control and difficulty understanding consequences. They don't know anything about food insecurity or poverty or homelessness or abuse.  They have been read to every day of their lives and love reading. It breaks my heart to think about the children who are most likely to end up in prison and what their life is like.   We all feel such great empathy for the dogs in the ASPCA ads who have been neglected and abused and are sitting in a shelter waiting for a home, but we fail to see our imprisoned population as a product of this same type of neglect and abuse. other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "dani-m08", "author_name": "dani_m08", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/dani-m08", "date": "2025-12-19", "text": "Did you take photos during the construction of your shower/shower pan? The way you've described how the pan was constructed doesn't make sense to me. There wouldn't be a \"shower pan\" - and then concrete  + thinset added.  The completed are is the shower pan. If a precast shower pan was used, it wouldn't need to have tile added. There are foam shower pans that are \"tile ready\"  that could be used - however, concrete would not have been added on top of it.  It would have tile installed with thinset. You need to ask your contractor if you have a traditional mud shower pan or a Kerdi (Schluter - or other brands) foam shower pan OR deck mud with a surface waterproof membrane. A traditional one is a \"water in - water out\" system.  The water that doesn't go down the drain will go through the grout and make it's way to the PVC waterproof liner.  The PVC liner will be over a sloped mix of sand/cement (the pre-slope) - and it will be sloped towards the drain.  The liner is then covered with another sloped layer of deck mud (which is porous to allow the water to drain through to the liner) - the water will be directed to the drain by the sloped deck mud underneath the pvc liner.  It is very important that the pvc liner is not installed flat on the subfloor - or water won't move towards the drain. A weeping drain will be used - it has weep holes in the drain under the tile where water (that went through the grout/tile) is able to enter to be drained.   The second method is a shower pan that has a surface waterproof membrane - it works in conjunction with a flange drain (not a weeping drain).  This type of shower pan will have only one sloped layer of deck mud + a surface waterproof membrane added over it.  Water does not go down to the deck mud - so, there are no weep holes or pvc liner (all water runs down the drain).   Ask your contractor how the pan was built (don't show him diagrams above - ask him to tell you exactly how it was constructed - otherwise, if he's dishonest, he could just point at one of the diagrams and tell you that's the way it was completed). If you have photos while the construction was happening, please add them.  Does your scope of work in your contract specify how the shower pan will be made?  Also, add a photo of your drain - most of the time you can tell whether it's a flange or weeping drain based upon the drain cover that has been installed.", "images": ["https://st.hzcdn.com/fimgs/7fa2258e0944eff1_5554-w240-h138-b0-p0--.jpg", "https://st.hzcdn.com/fimgs/cbd20af00944eff1_5555-w240-h127-b0-p0--.jpg"]}}

title: Water under vinyl plank flooring in basement | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "kdub0517", "author_name": "kdub0517", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/kdub0517", "date": "2025-12-22", "text": "Hi -- I had my hot water heater replaced in my basement and water was spilled on the floor during the work. It was cleaned up by the contractors, but the next day I noticed water coming up between the seams of the floating vinyl plank flooring where I was standing. I ended up removing the planks and there was water all over the entire concrete slab under the planks (the basement is small - about 15 by 15 feet). I was not able to remove the planks from under the water heater of course or under the washer dryer. I've been running a fan and dehumidifier since. The contractor who did the water heater says it'll be fine, just run the fan and it will dry and no mold will happen. I think it would be best to re-empty the water heater and lift it so I can remove the flooring from under it. Am I overreacting? Is it normal for water to spill on floor during water heater replacement? And then to seep through the floor planks and end up all under them in the whole room? Is it ok to leave some planks down since I got most of it out? (I don't really want to put the planks back in and would rather just have bare concrete in case of future water issues - it wasn't really fun removing those planks and carrying out of basement!)  Thank you for answers / advice on any or all of these questions!", "images": []}
other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "pfvwus-pf~1833970505", "author_name": "Minardi", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/professionals/pfvwus-pf~1833970505", "date": "2025-12-22", "text": "You don't need a water heat spill to have a ton of water underneath vinyl floors in a basement. title: Vaporvac!  Advice on lithium hand pruners...from the 'Novice.' | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "oldmoses", "author_name": "Moses, Pitt PA, cold W & hot-humid S, z6", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/oldmoses", "date": "2025-12-23", "text": "If you have hand trouble (arthritis, carpal tunnel, muscle weakness, etc....), a battery powered pruner is a Godsend. The first one I got was a battery powered pole pruner.  I didn't get it to prune branches/growth overhead up high, but to prune branches down low...spring pruning. This was when arthritis in my hands coupled with recovering from back to back hip replacements 5 yrs. ago, made the need to have a tool that could do major cuts, to 1.2\" diameter canes, close to the ground without me having to bend down. The one I got, on Amazon, was not expensive, < $100.00.  It was not a well known name brand...but it works great. The pruner separates from the pole and can be used by hand.  The battery is enclosed in the tool, not removable. The only thing I can add is, \"Get used to the weight of the pole pruner in use and even using the hand pruning section, separately.\"  The weight of the tools is a little annoying at first, but becomes inconsequential as skill develops. Last season I purchased a second hand pruning only unit, that has removable battery packs. Same as before, it was an Amazon generic brand, <$50.00, that works great.  I can do all aspects of spring pruning having both the pole pruner and hand pruner there in the garden with me. The cuts made by these battery powered tools are powerful, absolutely amazing.  It is 100% crucial to keep your free hand away from the cutting blades at all times.  When your hand holding the tool depresses the cut button, the tool cuts on command immediately and quickly....no time to get fingers out of the way AFTER the button's depressed!!!  These power tool, battery pruner units must be respected for the power they have.  Always keep your free hand clear of the cutting blades. Moses.", "images": []}

main_question: {"author_id": "melissaaipapa", "author_name": "Melissa Northern Italy zone 8", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/melissaaipapa", "date": "2025-12-23", "text": "Over the decades I've learned a good deal of patience in gardening.  Trees growing from seedlings, acorns even; tiny scraps of rose turning into mighty climbers; plants smashed or frozen to the ground that rebound in a few years.  All acceptable.  This year, though, I'm fretting, specifically about my cuttings.  Last October, for the first time in some years, I took cuttings of many of my Teas; I also collected suckers of several roses I wanted to have more plants of:  'William Lobb', 'Gros Choux de Hollande', 'F\u00e9licit\u00e9 Parmentier', 'Dupontii', and others.  For some reason, I think these should start sending out new growth now, in the depths of winter.  I go out and inspect them hopefully.  There they are, unmoving, at least as far as I can see, though I trust they're busy growing roots. The weather is vile now, gray and drippy, though fortunately not freezing; the days are the shortest of the year.  There's little incentive to go out into the wet unsightly garden and come back in with my shoes plastered with clay.  It'll be nice to see the sun again.  My helper got caught up on his work, good for my garden and his bank balance, not to mention his peace of mind.  Now we have a few days of rest--I've been overly busy the last couple of weeks--and, once I've recovered some energy, I can go out again in the garden and see what's going on among the snowdrops, sarcococcas, winter aconite, primroses, hazelnuts, and other trees that flower in winter. We could upsize the CFM of the blower, but from previous posts, it sounds like this would be relatively ineffective in capturing all of the effluent generated from steak searing or induction wok cooking. Realistically, I could widen the hood area to 42\" to overlap the cooktop area, but I'm not sure if I would be able to increase the depth of the hood. main_question: {"author_id": "anniedeighnaugh", "author_name": "Annie Deighnaugh", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/anniedeighnaugh", "date": "2025-12-26", "text": "I'm old enough to be irked by no one saying \"you're welcome\" any more after a thank you.  A lot say, \"thank you\" in return-- thank you for coming, thank you for having me so it's a reciprocal thing.  The 'no problem' is ok to me, similar to 'it's nothing' -- de rien, de nada -- usual enough and acceptable in my book.  But an 'mmhmm'?  Not good.  'Of course' grates on me, though it is a common response these days.  It's as if my appreciation of their effort means nothing to them. Rare is a \"my pleasure\". Reminds me of the old days when I remember Ann Landers complaining about people saying, \"Have a nice day.\"  I never understood that as I thought it was a lot better than \"hope you get run over by a truck.\"  But I guess she found it trite and insincere. Today I came across this article that the younger folks actually think \"you're welcome\" implies that you weren't really welcome at all, or that it entails sarcasm or a sense of obligation.  Really?  I just thought it was the polite answer.  And that's why they don't say it. title: alkaline water and rooting | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "daninthedirt", "author_name": "daninthedirt (USDA 9a, HZ9, CentTX, Sunset z30, Cfa)", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/daninthedirt", "date": "2025-12-27", "text": "Here in the Austin area, the pH of tap water is 9.5. Zowee. Lake water is 8.5, but they kick the pH up to precipitate out minerals, so the water tastes better. Over the years, I've had trouble rooting in water for propagation. You know, plunk a stem in water and wait for roots to form. Turns out pH>8.5 is actually destructive to roots, and also inhibits nutrient takeup. It's called alkaline stress. Hydroponic users always keep their water slightly acidic. So why do things grow well in our soil irrigated with our tap water? Because our soil  buffers whatever acidic or alkaline liquids are dumped on it to make, for me, pH 7.8. So, from now on, I'm using distilled water (or rain water) for rooting. The lesson is to be aware of your tap water pH when you're using it to root. In Texas, distilled water is free. You just catch the condensate from your a/c in the summer.", "images": []}

title: Cashless society | Houzz Forum
main_question: {"author_id": "palimpsest", "author_name": "palimpsest", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/palimpsest", "date": "2025-12-28", "text": "On the one hand, some restaurants are starting to surcharge for using a credit card, to encourage people to pay in cash. (I was actually in a restaurant in Manhattan on Christmas even and did see someone pay a check of a couple hundred dollars with cash, so I guess people still do.) On the other hand I wanted something other than a $20 to leave for housekeeping and when I went to the front desk of the hotel, they did not have a cashbox, one of the guys at the counter checked his own wallet and happened to have the change. (So the expectation seems to be that so few people use cash that there is no need to have a supply of change). ------ And another thing. I think there is such a thing as over-gentrification. In the West Village -Meat Packing district, there is a condo unit for sale @ $85 Million. And there is a Gucci right across the street from what used to be a hot-sheets hotel/notorious bar that had a woman in a bikini inside a rolling set of bars pacing back and forth with a sign that said to stop arresting s*x workers. And now an Hermes nearby, too ($200 Hermes bandaid, anyone?) On the one hand, you can safely walk through the neighborhood at night. (well, you kinda could before). On the other hand, nobody can afford to move into the neighborhood unless they are wealthy or can get into someone's long term rent controlled apartment.", "images": []}

other_comments: {"Comment 1": {"author_id": "3onthetree", "author_name": "3onthetree", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/3onthetree", "date": "2025-12-29", "text": "The best approach to attic ventilation is passive ventilation, low to high across the entire underside of each plane of roof. Clay tile over cleats, which is then over sheathing with roofing underlayment, is good for the sheathing and tile, but doesn't address the attic. When you need to rethink attic ventilation, my first question is, what is the problem you are experiencing? Condensation or mold - find the culprit (too little ventilation, bath exhaust, insufficient insulation, no air sealing, blocked vents, etc). Just higher temps - attics can easily be around 20F-30F higher than outside temp, and that is perfectly fine. O'Hagin vents were created to solve a problem. Namely, when you can't get enough low or high soffit venting and need an alternate location. The downside is they move more air in spots, not across the entire roof plane. There are many houses where gable vents might be adequately performing, each house is a bit different and applying a broad brush for optimal venting may not be necessary because of other details that do not work for the house.", "images": []}}

main_question: {"author_id": "webuser-209235904", "author_name": "Riccardo", "author_url": "https://www.houzz.com/user/webuser-209235904", "date": "2025-12-31", "text": "I have recently bought a 1930\u2019s property and what was the outhouse toilet has been incorporated into the property so that it\u2019s inside. The back and right walls are single outside walls. Is it possible to plasterboard the outside walls, do something with the ceiling and raise the flooring with a suspended floor to match the level of the rest of the property?", "images": ["https://st.hzcdn.com/fimgs/5a22da3a095558bb_0958-w500-h666-b0-p0--.jpg"]}

Ideally you would stud the walls to control damp/cold and to make the finished walls straight.   This will be 10cm which is probably a 15% reduction in the width of the total space.    You can get insulated plasterboard which is a thinner way of achieving a finished room.   Although these start at 12mm thick this delivers very modest insulation and likely you would specify one thicker such as 62mm-72mm.   Adhesive could add up to 15mm for uneven walls The work to the floor and walls would also require you to move the toilet and therefore it will be a lot of expense for such a small area and the same spend elsewhere is the property will likely give you a bigger/ more impressive return on the money spent. Quest for Zest - this was an impulse-buy for me this year and it has really knocked my socks off in its first year. I love the ruffly flowers, fragrance, and it really has a lovely bush shape.
